title: Getting Started & Variables
description: Learn the basics of Python, including printing to the screen, variables, strings, and numbers, mirroring Chapters 1 and 2 of Python Crash Course.

lessons.title: Hello World!
lessons.description: Run your first Python program and learn what really happens when you run a file.

stages.title: What Happens When You Run Your Code
stages.description: Understanding the Python Interpreter and the print() function.
stages.instructions:
A long-held belief in the programming world is that printing a `Hello world!` message to the screen as your first program in a new language will bring you luck.

In Python, you can write the Hello World program in one line:

### Syntax:
```python
print("Hello world!")
```

When you run this code, your editor runs the file through the Python interpreter, which reads through the program and determines what each word in the program means. For example, when the interpreter sees the word `print`, it prints to the screen whatever is inside the parentheses.

stages.title: Your First Program
stages.description: Write a program that prints a message to the screen.
stages.instructions:
Try to print the message `Hello Python world!` exactly as shown below.

### Sample Output:
```text

```
stages.hint: Make sure you use double quotes inside the print() function parentheses and match the spelling exactly.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.description: Learn how to store and change data using variables.

stages.title: Naming and Using Variables
stages.description: Adding variables to your programs.
stages.instructions:
Let's try using a variable. Every variable holds a value, which is the information associated with that variable.

### Example:
```python
message = "Hello Python world!"
print(message)
```

When you're using variables in Python, you need to adhere to a few rules and guidelines:
- Variable names can contain only letters, numbers, and underscores.
- Spaces are not allowed in variable names, but underscores can be used to separate words (e.g., `greeting_message`).
- Variable names should be short but descriptive.

lessons.title: Strings
lessons.description: Learn to manipulate text data using string methods.

stages.title: Changing Case in a String
stages.description: Using string methods like title(), upper(), and lower().
stages.instructions:
A string is simply a series of characters. Anything inside quotes is considered a string in Python.

One of the simplest tasks you can do with strings is change the case of the words in a string using methods. A method is an action that Python can perform on a piece of data.

### Example:
```python
name = "ada lovelace"
print(name.title())
print(name.upper())
```

`title()` displays each word in titlecase, where each word begins with a capital letter. `upper()` changes a string to all uppercase.

lessons.title: Numbers
lessons.description: Learn to work with integers and floats.

stages.title: Integers and Floats
stages.description: Using math operations in Python.
stages.instructions:
Numbers are used quite often in programming. You can add (+), subtract (-), multiply (*), and divide (/) integers in Python.

### Example:
```python
print(2 + 3)
print(3 ** 2) # Exponents are represented by two asterisks
```

Python calls any number with a decimal point a float. You can combine operations, and Python supports the order of operations.

title: Introducing Lists
description: Learn what lists are and how to work with the individual elements in a list, mirroring Chapter 3 of Python Crash Course.

lessons.title: What is a List?
lessons.description: Learn how to define a list and access its elements.

stages.title: Accessing Elements in a List
stages.description: Using index positions to access list items.
stages.instructions:
A list is a collection of items in a particular order. In Python, square brackets (`[]`) indicate a list, and individual elements are separated by commas.

### Example:
```python
bicycles = ['trek', 'cannondale', 'redline', 'specialized']
```

Lists are ordered collections, so you can access any element by telling Python the position, or index, of the item. **Index Positions Start at 0, Not 1.**

### Example Access:
```python
print(bicycles[0].title()) # Outputs 'Trek'
print(bicycles[-1]) # Outputs the last item ('specialized')
```

lessons.title: Modifying Lists
lessons.description: Learn how to change, add, and remove elements from a list.

stages.title: Appending and Removing
stages.description: Using append(), insert(), del, pop(), and remove().
stages.instructions:
Most lists you create will be dynamic, meaning you'll build a list and then add and remove elements from it as your program runs.

### Adding Elements:
- `.append('ducati')`: Adds to the end of the list.
- `.insert(0, 'ducati')`: Adds to a specific position.

### Removing Elements:
- `del motorcycles[0]`: Removes an item if you know its index.
- `.pop()`: Removes the last item in a list, but lets you work with it.
- `.remove('ducati')`: Removes an item by value.

title: Working with Lists

lessons.title: Looping Through an Entire List
lessons.description: Using for loops to automate repetitive tasks.

stages.title: The For Loop
stages.description: Taking the same action with every item in a list.
stages.instructions:
When you want to do the same action with every item in a list, you can use Python's `for` loop.

### Example:
```python
magicians = ['alice', 'david', 'carolina']
for magician in magicians:
    print(magician.title() + ", that was a great trick!")
print("Thank you, everyone.")
```

Python uses indentation to determine when one line of code is connected to the line above it. Any lines of code after the `for` loop that are not indented are executed once without repetition.

lessons.title: Conditional Tests
lessons.description: Learn to write expressions that evaluate to True or False.

stages.title: Equality and Inequality
stages.description: Comparing values in Python.
stages.instructions:
At the heart of every `if` statement is an expression that can be evaluated as `True` or `False` and is called a conditional test.

### Examples:
- **Equality**: `car == 'bmw'`
- **Inequality**: `car != 'audi'`
- **Numerical**: `age >= 18`
- **Multiple Conditions**: `age >= 21 and age_1 >= 21` or `age >= 21 or age_1 >= 21`
- **In a List**: `'mushrooms' in requested_toppings`

title: Dictionaries
description: Learn how to use Python dictionaries to connect related pieces of information, mirroring Chapter 6.

stages.title: A Simple Dictionary
stages.description: Accessing and modifying key-value pairs.
stages.instructions:
A dictionary in Python is a collection of key-value pairs. Each key is connected to a value, and you can use a key to access the value associated with that key.

### Example:
```python
alien_0 = {'color': 'green', 'points': 5}
print(alien_0['color']) # Prints 'green'
```

You can add new pairs dynamically:
```python
alien_0['x_position'] = 0
```

title: User Input and while Loops
description: Learn to keep programs running as long as certain conditions are true, mirroring Chapter 7.

lessons.title: Introducing while Loops
lessons.description: Run blocks of code repeatedly while a condition is True.

stages.title: The while Loop in Action
stages.description: Using while to count or act until a condition changes.
stages.instructions:
The `for` loop takes a collection of items and executes a block of code once for each item in the collection. In contrast, the `while` loop runs as long as, or while, a certain condition is true.

### Example:
```python
current_number = 1
while current_number <= 5:
    print(current_number)
    current_number += 1
```

You can use the `break` statement to exit a loop immediately, or `continue` to return to the beginning of the loop.

title: Functions
description: Write named blocks of code that do one specific job, mirroring Chapter 8.

lessons.title: Defining a Function
lessons.description: Learn to write your own functions and pass arguments to them.

stages.title: Arguments and Parameters
stages.description: Passing information to a function.
stages.instructions:
Functions are named blocks of code that are designed to do one specific job. When you want to perform a particular task that you've defined in a function, you *call* the name of the function.

### Example:
```python
def greet_user(username):
    """Display a simple greeting."""
    print("Hello, " + username.title() + "!")

greet_user('jesse')
```

The variable `username` in the definition is a *parameter*. The value `'jesse'` passed in the call is an *argument*.

title: Classes
description: Learn object-oriented programming to model real-world situations, mirroring Chapter 9.

lessons.title: Creating and Using a Class
lessons.description: Learn how to define a class and create instances from it.

stages.title: The __init__() Method
stages.description: Initializing object attributes.
stages.instructions:
In object-oriented programming you write *classes* that represent real-world things and situations, and you create *objects* based on these classes.

### Example:
```python
class Dog():
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def sit(self):
        print(self.name.title() + " is now sitting.")

my_dog = Dog('willie', 6)
my_dog.sit()
```
The `__init__()` method is a special method Python runs automatically whenever we create a new instance based on the class. Variables prefixed with `self` are available to every method in the class and are called *attributes*.
